issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s right under a government grant restricting a landholder from evicting tenants is preserved by the statutory protection for rights arising from a grant.
material_facts: The government confirmed the landholder’s grant subject to a condition that he would not evict the cultivators.
The tenants claimed the benefit of that condition in resisting the landholder’s application for land for personal cultivation.
The landholder had accepted the condition attached to the grant.
issues.conclusion: The tenants’ right under the condition was a right arising out of a grant and was protected; the statutory protection for tenants was not limited to rights arising from a grant made directly by a landholder to a tenant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18 of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951 preserves a tenant’s rights and privileges arising out of a grant or otherwise, and the word “grant” includes a government grant to a Girasdar. Although section 3 gives the Act overriding effect over inconsistent instruments, section 18 preserves these independently arising tenant rights.

predicates.land_reform_tenancy_dispute: The dispute concerns the rights of tenants and a landholder under a land-reform regime.
predicates.tenant_privilege_arises_from_grant: A tenant’s claimed privilege arises from a grant subject to a condition intended to benefit the tenant.

issues.definition: When a land-reform tenancy dispute concerns a tenant privilege arising from a grant, that grant-based privilege remains protected.

issues.legal_issue: A landholder who accepted a grant condition prohibiting eviction cannot obtain a statutory personal-cultivation allotment that would enable eviction in breach of the condition.
material_facts: The landholder accepted the government’s confirmation of his grant subject to a condition that he would not evict the tenants.
He applied for an allotment of land for personal cultivation, which would enable him to evict tenants from the allotted land.
The tenants did not have chav or buta hak, but their right not to be evicted arose from the grant condition.
The revenue tribunal dismissed the application, and the High Court declined to interfere.
issues.conclusion: The application for allotment was incompetent because an allotment order could not limit or abridge the tenants’ rights under the grant condition. The appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 18, 19 and 20 of the Saurashtra Land Reforms Act, 1951 do not permit a personal-cultivation allotment that would abridge a tenant’s preserved rights. Section 20(2) provides for an allotment order, and section 20(4) makes that order the basis on which a Girasdar may obtain possession; those provisions do not override section 18. The appellant accepted the grant subject to its conditions and was bound by them. The Court also referred to State of Saurashtra v. Jamadar Mohammad Abdulla for the proposition that annulment of a grant by the government would be an act of State not open to challenge before municipal tribunals.

predicates.statutory_personal_cultivation_allotment: A landholder applies under a statutory scheme for an allotment of land for personal cultivation.
predicates.accepted_grant_forbids_eviction: The landholder accepted a grant subject to a condition that the tenants must not be evicted.
predicates.allotment_would_enable_eviction: The requested allotment would enable the landholder to obtain possession by evicting tenants.
predicates.tenants_have_grant_based_non_eviction_ri: The tenants have a right not to be evicted that arises from the grant condition.

issues.definition: If a landholder seeks a personal-cultivation allotment that would enable eviction despite an accepted grant condition protecting the tenants from eviction, the application is incompetent.
